title.en: Workbook Practice: Two Stories about Flying
Rules, phrasal verbs, and the passive voice

text.en: From A.G. Gardiner's 'All about a Dog' to phrasal verbs and passive voice, Unit 3 of Words and Expressions 2 sharpens how you describe actions and punctuate paragraphs.

Unit 3 reviews 'His First Flight' and 'The Black Aeroplane', then presents A.G. Gardiner's essay 'All about a Dog'.
In 'All about a Dog', a bus conductor insists on following the rule to the letter on a freezing night, refusing to move the bus until a woman takes her little Pekinese dog to the open top deck.
Vocabulary teaches forming adverbs from adjectives (e.g., angry -> angrily, vague -> vaguely, hurry -> hurriedly) and using negative prefixes like 'im-' (immovable).
Grammar covers Phrasal Verbs (verb + preposition/adverb with a new meaning, like 'walk away', 'put away', 'put out') and the Passive Voice.
In Passive Voice, the receiver of the action becomes the subject (e.g., 'Ramesh painted the walls' -> 'The walls were painted by Ramesh').
Editing practises capital letters, commas, and full stops in a paragraph about UFOs, and sentence unscrambling.
Unit 3 explores rules versus kindness in A.G. Gardiner's 'All about a Dog'.
The conductor had the law on his side, yet his rigid attitude made all the passengers suffer in the cold.
To form adverbs from adjectives ending in -y, change -y to -ily, like 'angry' becoming 'angrily'.
Phrasal verbs like 'put out' (extinguish) or 'walk away' (leave) have meanings beyond the single verb.
In the passive voice, 'be + past participle' shifts focus from the doer to the action's receiver.
Always check punctuation: proper nouns and sentence starts need capitals, and complete thoughts need full stops.

problem.en: Change to passive voice (Simple Past): 'The volcanic eruption in Mt. Etna / destroy / many houses and lives.'

text.en: Identify the receiver ('Many houses and lives') and make it the subject.

why.en: Passive voice puts the object of the active verb first.

text.en: Use Simple Past passive ('were + past participle'): 'Many houses and lives were destroyed by the volcanic eruption in Mt. Etna.'

why.en: 'Many houses and lives' is plural, so use 'were destroyed'.

prompt.en: Explain the difference between active and passive voice, and give an example of a phrasal verb.

requiredIdeas.en: Active voice focuses on the doer; passive voice focuses on the receiver using be + past participle
Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a preposition or adverb to create a new meaning
Rules should be applied with common sense and empathy

commonMisconceptions.en: Forgetting to match 'was/were' to singular/plural subjects in passive voice

points.en: Adverbs often end in -ly (angrily, vaguely, hurriedly), and prefixes like im- form antonyms.
Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a preposition/adverb (e.g., put away, put out).
Passive voice uses 'be + past participle' when the receiver of the action is the subject.
Proper punctuation (capitals, commas, full stops) makes long paragraphs clear.
